nameStory: This tiny spider doesn't have a widely-used common name, so it goes by its scientific name Agyneta fabra. The genus name 'Agyneta' comes from Greek meaning 'without a female' - though this doesn't mean there are no females, just that early scientists had trouble finding them! The species name 'fabra' means 'craftsman' in Latin, honoring these spiders' intricate sheet web construction skills.
description: Agyneta fabra is a minuscule sheet weaver spider, so small you might mistake it for a speck of dust at first glance. These tiny arachnids are part of the dwarf weaver family, living up to their name by being among the smallest spiders you'll encounter in New England. They're typically dark-colored with a compact, rounded abdomen and relatively long legs for their body size. Despite their diminutive stature, they're skilled web builders, creating delicate horizontal sheet webs close to the ground.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely small - often less than 2mm in body length, easily mistaken for a tiny beetle or even a crumb when not moving

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Creates delicate, flat sheet webs stretched horizontally near ground level, feeling almost silky-smooth when accidentally brushed

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact and rounded with a relatively small cephalothorax (front section) and bulbous abdomen that looks almost bead-like

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Generally dark brown to blackish coloration, sometimes with a slightly glossy sheen that catches light

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves quickly when disturbed, often dropping from web or scurrying to hide under nearby debris

habitat: Look for Agyneta fabra in leaf litter, low vegetation, and grassy areas throughout New England's forests and meadows. They prefer moist microhabitats where they can string their sheet webs between grass stems, fallen leaves, or low-growing plants. You'll have the best luck spotting their webs in areas with some shelter from wind, like forest edges or protected woodland clearings.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, beginning to construct their characteristic sheet webs in protected spots among emerging vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most commonly found on their webs. This is the best time to spot them, though you'll need to look very carefully due to their tiny size.
seasonality.fall: Adults may still be active in early fall, with some individuals persisting until first frost. Egg laying likely occurs during this period.
seasonality.winter: Overwinters in protected locations, possibly as eggs or very young spiders hidden deep in leaf litter and soil crevices.

funFact: These spiders are so small that a gentle breeze can actually lift them off their webs and carry them through the air - a phenomenon called 'ballooning' that allows them to colonize new areas without ever touching the ground!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other tiny sheet weaver spiders in the same family, but the combination of extremely small size, dark coloration, and horizontal sheet webs helps narrow it down. Remember: if it's smaller than your pinky nail and has a flat web, you're likely looking at a dwarf weaver of some kind.
contextualKnowledge: The Linyphiidae family (sheet weavers and dwarf weavers) contains some of the most abundant spiders on Earth, yet they're rarely noticed by people due to their tiny size. Many species in this family are so small they're primarily studied by specialists with microscopes.
compareHints: Since this appears to be the only Agyneta species commonly found in New England, compare it with other small Linyphiidae family members. Agyneta fabra tends to be darker and more compact than many related dwarf weavers, with a particularly rounded abdomen shape. Its sheet webs are typically positioned closer to the ground than those of many similar species.
